picked.t: Vietnam's $13B airport Long Thanh short of skilled workers two months before opening
picked.body: In a report sent to the government on Oct. 20, the ministry said several parts of the airport are behind schedule, with partial operations due to begin on Dec. 24. Airports Corporation of Vietnam (ACV) is the investor in component project 3, which covers the airport's essential facilities and is 86.03% complete by value of work done. Of its 12 construction packages under way, eight are expected to finish in December. The four at risk are the airport's internal roads and technical infrastructure, the passenger terminal, Cargo Terminal No. 1 and its auxiliary works, and the parking building. Work on the passenger terminal is 86.85% complete, with electrical and mechanical installation at 96.2%. Its structure is finished, but a large amount of work remains. Contractors there are struggling to bring in engineers, welders and specialized equipment installers, and slow paperwork has also affected payments and work on site. The terminal has 51 integrated load-test scenarios to check how its power, water supply and drainage, air conditioning, ventilation, firefighting and specialized equipment systems work together, but 16 have yet to be approved. Under the approved scenarios, the contractor has so far tested only the power supply, lighting and public address systems. The other systems have not been tested, and the investor has yet to set a date for finishing the tests. The internal roads and technical infrastructure package still has a large volume of work left but lacks enough construction workers, which the ministry called the main reason it cannot speed up. The remaining work also needs about 100,000 tons of asphalt concrete, but supply is severely short, making it hard to finish on schedule. At the airport's energy center, equipment has not been fully installed or test-run, either individually or together with other systems under load. Its readiness is a prerequisite for operating the passenger terminal, and the ministry said the target of completing it in November carries many risks. The ministry blamed the delays at all four packages on contractors not deploying as many workers and technical staff as they had committed to the investor. Slow paperwork has also left a large backlog of completed but unpaid work, and many packages have been paid little relative to the work done, affecting progress. The ministry called on ACV to push contractors to deploy enough workers, machinery, equipment, fuel and materials as committed. Where they fall short, ACV must determine who is responsible and act under the contracts to keep the project on schedule. ACV must also quickly resolve problems with payment for completed work and with changes to materials and equipment from the approved designs. Long Thanh, Vietnam's largest airport by area, covers about 5,000 ha in Dong Nai, some 40 km east of Ho Chi Minh City, and has a total investment of VND336.63 trillion (US$13 billion). Its first phase is designed to handle 25 million passengers and 1.2 million tons of cargo a year.

picked.t: Vietnamese businesses in France fear ruin as riots disrupt livelihoods
picked.body: On Oct. 17, while on a business trip in Madrid, Spain, Hanoi native Ha Linh, 34, constantly received photos and videos sent by staff and neighbors from her family’s nail salon in central Paris . On the streets around her shop, rioters smashed storefronts, set vehicles on fire, and built barricades with public bicycles. Many shops closed, but several clothing and shoe stores nearby had their windows shattered and merchandise looted. "I was on edge watching those scenes. I was afraid that the money and effort we’ve put into building the shop over three years could be wiped out," Linh says. The wave of protests in France began in September, when groups of students started blocking schools to demand better educational conditions. The movement subsequently spread as labor unions and various social groups took to the streets to protest rising fuel prices, high living costs, and cuts in public services. Although most demonstrations were peaceful, riots spiraled out of control in many areas of Paris, Marseille, Lyon, and other major cities. Masked groups dressed in black set cars on fire, torched buildings, and looted shops. On Oct.17, an estimated 550,000 to 800,000 people took to the streets nationwide. The French Ministry of the Interior reported that authorities arrested over 2,500 people. Nearly 1,000 police officers and gendarmes were injured. Alain Di Crescenzo, president of the French Chamber of Commerce, said street violence has affected more than 2,000 businesses and caused hundreds of millions of euros in damage. Having lived in France for 11 years and witnessed numerous protests, Linh says the threat this time is far greater because her shop, her family's main source of income, is at the epicenter of the rioting. Three years ago, she quit her job in the IT sector and, together with her husband, invested €80,000-90,000 (US$89,900-101,000) and took bank loans to open the shop. They now pay €3,000 a month on rent, salaries for four to six employees, taxes, and for other costs. On Oct. 17, her salon remained open to serve clients who had booked in advance. But for safety’s sake, the staff pulled the shutter almost all the way down to the ground, leaving only a tiny gap to observe the outside. "When clients arrived, they had to stand close to the door so the staff could see their feet, verify their identity, crack the door slightly to let them in, and immediately slam it shut again," she recalls. Once inside, many clients were afraid to leave after getting their nails done for fear of the violence on the streets. That evening, many metro stations closed and roads were blocked, forcing the salon staff to take detours of over 10 kilometers to catch rides home. Though not vandalized, the business suffered. Since early October, the number of customers has decreased by 20%. On weekends, when there were riots, the appointment cancellation rate was 50%. Beyond security concerns, Parisians have also begun cutting back on non-essential services. "In the past, regulars would return every three weeks, but now they return every 5 or 6 weeks. Parisians love beauty care, but when the economy and security are unstable, they budget much more carefully for every expense," Linh shares. More than 460 kilometers away, Tran Doan Huong, 30, owner of a Vietnamese restaurant in Lyon, has also had to change how he operates since early October. In the last three weeks, the central area of Lyon has frequently seen bricks, smoke bombs, burned cars, and shattered bus shelters. Huong remains vigilant when going out, taking detours to avoid crowded gathering spots. His greatest concern is that the restaurant he opened at the end of 2024 might be broken into and smashed by rioters. As various establishments from hair salons to bars and eateries have been randomly attacked, he decided to move all valuable equipment and belongings out of the restaurant at closing time every day. On Oct. 17, he gave all his staff a day off on safety grounds and came to the restaurant alone to guard the place while selling only a few fast-food items. "Every morning, when I go to the restaurant to open up, I only dare breathe a sigh of relief once I see the place is still intact after a night of protests," he says. He says the rioting, but also rising fuel and living costs, makes people chary of dining out, and his restaurant's revenues have plummeted as a result. His plans to open a branch are currently on hold, and he is searching for areas farther from the center and with fewer demonstrations. "I just hope the situation in France stabilizes soon so that people can live and work in peace," he says. Many Vietnamese students in France have had their routines disrupted. Ngoc Han, a student working part-time at a Vietnamese restaurant in Lyon, says she has to check public transit alerts, her school schedule, and protest maps every morning before stepping out of her apartment. picked.t: Beijer Electronics, AVA Vietnam partner with HCM-UTE to advance industrial automation education
picked.body: The partnership covers technical training, student projects, research and practical learning, aiming to help students develop engineering skills relevant to manufacturing. The agreement was signed at HCM-UTE, with representatives from all three organizations attending. The collaboration will combine Beijer Electronics' expertise in industrial automation, human-machine interface (HMI) technology, digitalization and smart manufacturing with HCM-UTE's academic programs in electrical and electronics engineering and automation. Activities will include technical workshops, research projects and industry engagement to give students greater exposure to industrial technologies and their manufacturing applications. Beijer Electronics also expect the partnership may create future opportunities for student internships, industry exposure, and student exchange activities. It said these initiatives could help students gain practical experience and better understand the skills required in the industrial automation sector. Ali Rezaei, Vice President of Global Sales and Marketing at Beijer Electronics, said the partnership would help prepare engineering students for changes in manufacturing. According to him, it is essential that students gain exposure not only to technology but also to real-world industrial challenges and opportunities. "Through the collaboration with HCM-UTE and AVA, we are committed to sharing knowledge, experience, and innovation, helping the next generation of engineers build the skills and confidence needed to drive meaningful progress in our industry," Ali Rezaei said. At the event, Beijer Electronics also held a seminar for students and faculty members on its products and technologies, as well as developments in industrial automation and smart manufacturing. The three organizations inaugurated the Beijer Electronics Lab, which will support hands-on training and collaboration between the university and industry. Associate Professor Le My Ha, Dean of HCM-UTE's Faculty of Electrical and Electronics Engineering, said the university is committed to developing engineering professionals who possess both strong academic foundations and practical industry skills. This partnership with Beijer Electronics and AVA can create valuable opportunities for their students and faculty to engage with advanced industrial technologies, collaborative research, and hands-on learning experiences. "We believe this cooperation will contribute significantly to preparing future engineers for the evolving demands of modern manufacturing and automation," he said. He added that the cooperation would help prepare graduates for changing requirements in manufacturing and automation. Beijer Electronics develops technologies for industrial visualization, automation and digitalization, including solutions for machine operations and manufacturing processes. The partners plan to expand technical training, research cooperation and practical learning opportunities, strengthening links between HCM-UTE and industry while supporting the development of skilled workers for Vietnam's manufacturing and automation sectors.

picked.t: Companies increasingly require employees to use up annual leave
picked.body: Dr. Le Trung Hieu, who directs HR management development at the School of Business Administration at the Vietnam National University, Hanoi, says persuading workers to exhaust their leave before financial books close is a trend adopted from foreign enterprises in the country. He listed four reasons for employers making using up leave mandatory. Financially, untaken vacation days sit on corporate ledgers as accrued liabilities or projected costs that require employees to take leave before accounts are closed for the financial year. Legally, it also keeps companies compliant with occupational health and safety codes and shields corporate reputations from fallout tied to workplace burnout. Operationally, vacations give employees room to recover while stress-testing whether a company's internal systems can function seamlessly when individual workers are absent. For companies compensating employees based on project output rather than billable hours, having staff take time off also reduces overheads, trimming costs on electricity, water, office catering, and basic supplies. Internationally, several countries hold businesses to strict standards regarding vacation rights; Germany requires workers to use their full allowance within the calendar year, granting extensions into the following quarter only under pressing circumstances, while Japan allows unused days to roll over for up to two years. "The Federal Labor Court in Germany requires employers to urge staff to take their statutory leave, with authorities handing down administrative fines of up to 30,000 euros (approx. VND810 million) or even pursuing criminal charges against companies that block legitimate time off," Stoffers told VnExpress. Hieu noted that the practice is standard among multinational corporations answering to parent companies in Europe, North America, and Japan; large joint ventures and publicly listed firms facing regular audits; and financial institutions spanning banking and insurance. Doan Huy, who heads sales at a Hanoi-based conglomerate (subject wished to stay anonymous), said his company routinely audits leave balances and alerts employees so they can plan ahead. The company only asks that staff limit consecutive absences to three days during urgent rollouts and insists on thorough handovers beforehand. A bank branch manager in the northern port city of Hai Phong confirmed that his office actively encourages vacations as long as project deadlines remain secure. For management-level personnel, taking all allotted annual leave is mandatory, during which headquarters sends interim coverage to manage daily duties. "Many managers barely touch half their time off because of crushing workloads, so this hard rule forces them to step away and recharge," the branch manager said. Pham Tuan Phuc, managing director of the executive recruiting firm Robert Walters Vietnam, observed that major corporations have established clear pipelines for requesting time off and handing off projects. "Many firms view downtime as a routine part of daily operations, not as a sign of slacking off," Phuc explained. Annual leave policies have become a trending topic across social media, sparking hundreds of posts and commentary. Alongside grievances about stubborn managers preventing them from taking days off, many workers are also reporting the exact opposite dilemma: being pressured or forced to fully use their leave. Professor Andreas Stoffers, a Southeast Asian business specialist at FOM University of Applied Sciences in Germany, observed to VnExpress that having to push employees into taking leave stems from deference to authority, a culture where staff rarely take initiative without top-down permission, and a stubborn workplace tendency to equate loyalty with face time at the office. In Vietnam, exposure to foreign work environments—notably Japanese and South Korean corporate cultures—has introduced rigid workplace habits. Meanwhile, an oversupply of college graduates has driven many into positions below their qualifications, steadily eroding basic employee protections and benefits. Yet that culture is beginning to turn. While the practice serves companies well, Hieu cautioned that forcing employees into last-minute leave crunches at year-end can backfire. Lingering anxieties about unfinished deadlines often lead workers to log in reluctantly from home, ending in exhaustion. He urged businesses to adopt flexible frameworks, allowing staff to schedule extended time off well in advance, roll over days, or receive financial compensation when ongoing deliverables cannot be put on pause.

picked.t: Ho Chi Minh City plans public schools with higher English bar than most Vietnamese universities
picked.body: The city's Department of Education and Training is collecting feedback on the criteria, quality assurance conditions and education services for the new type of school, set out in a draft decision for the municipal People's Committee. A high-quality school is defined as one that is academically strong, with better staff and educational results than any existing model. Preschool teachers, for example, normally need only a college diploma, but at high-quality preschools 70% would need a university degree or higher. The differences are clearest at secondary and high schools, where every teacher would be able to communicate in English and at least 30% would reach level 4 or above on Vietnam's six-level framework, equivalent to B2 on the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages. At least 85% of secondary school teachers and 60% of high school teachers would hold a master's or doctorate, where a bachelor's degree is normally enough. Secondary school students would have to reach B1 English and high school students B2, while most universities in Vietnam currently require B1 English for graduation. All secondary school students would also be expected to win places at public high schools or international schools, and all high school students to enter a university or college in Vietnam or study abroad. Regular schools face none of these requirements. High-quality preschools would have to be recognized as meeting national standards at level 2 or higher and have rooms equipped with modern technology. Children would be introduced to English through an integrated program, in an English-speaking environment with cultural exchanges, performances, reading and music in English. High-quality primary schools would have classes of 35 students and separate rooms for music, art, foreign languages and computer science. All their teachers would hold a university degree, with half qualified above that level. All would speak English fluently, and 30% would be able to teach in it. Primary teachers in integrated programs would need a B2 English certificate, and those teaching subjects in English a C1 certificate or higher. At least 80% of pupils would be taught to swim safely, and at least 60% would meet international standards or earn international certificates in English and computer science. At secondary and high schools, classes would have 30 students attending two sessions a day, and every teacher would be digitally proficient. All students there would be taught to swim safely and prevent drowning, and half would hold international English certificates. The department said there is currently no set of criteria for assessing high-quality schools, while residents expect more from their schools and want students equipped with foreign language, digital and AI skills, STEM education and skills for international integration. It said a growing share of parents are willing to pay for supplementary and advanced education services for their children, but gave no figures. Besides its mainstream public schools, Ho Chi Minh City, Vietnam's most populous city with more than 14 million people, already has more than 80 schools from preschool to high school running an advanced, regional and international integration model. Those schools charge more than VND1.7 million (US$66) per student a month.

picked.t: 11 school sanitation facilities inaugurated in Son La
picked.body: Opella Vietnam and its Enterogermina brand funded 10 facilities in Chieng Khuong, Muong Lam, Huoi Mot, Muong Hung and Bo Sinh communes. BW Industrial funded the remaining facility at Nam Ty Ethnic Boarding Secondary School in Nam Ty Commune. Designed by Vietnam Construction Consulting Corporation to meet Ministry of Education and Training standards, each facility has six to 12 stalls, separate sections for boys and girls, toilets, handwashing stations, water systems and septic tanks. Signs promote proper toilet use and handwashing. The new facilities are expected to ease overcrowding and improve sanitation for students. At Bo Sinh Ethnic Boarding Primary and Secondary School, more than 860 students previously shared 10 makeshift toilets with tin walls that were built in 2000 and lacked septic systems. Wastewater flowed into open pits, producing strong odors that reached nearby classrooms. Principal Nguyen Chi Cong said many students had held in their needs during school hours or gone to nearby hills to relieve themselves. "Especially older girls often felt uncomfortable due to the lack of privacy. Now we have standard toilets, and both students and teachers feel very happy," he said. At Nam Ty Ethnic Boarding Secondary School, the new facility will also serve more than 800 students. The old toilets were overcrowded and in poor condition, with students often jostling for space after breaks. Nguyen Cong Vien, chairman of the Chieng Khuong Commune People's Committee and former head of the Song Ma District Education and Training Office, said school sanitation had become a priority after temporary classroom needs were addressed. Since 2023, Hope Foundation has helped build nearly 200 toilet rooms in the area and mobilized additional support from other organizations. This year's project also includes teacher training conducted by the Center for Children and Development (CCD) and sponsored by Opella Vietnam. The training equips teachers with knowledge and methods to teach hygiene and sustain the program's impact after the project ends. Following the handover, the project will continue working with primary and secondary schools in Son La to help students develop good hygiene habits through short videos and hands-on practice at the new facilities. Organizers will assess the program's effectiveness through surveys conducted before and after the activities. At the inauguration ceremony, students took part in traditional folk games, including pao throwing, tug-of-war and stick pushing, as well as drawing activities. The activities were designed to encourage physical activity and reinforce daily hygiene habits.
